name: Quorums
intent: Choose how many replicas must answer a write and a read so that every read overlaps with the latest write, trading consistency, latency and availability.
scenario: A key-value store keeps each item on 5 replicas. A write is acknowledged by some of them, a read asks some of them, and replicas can be slow or down. How many does each operation need to wait for?
problem: Waiting for every replica on every operation is slow and fails when any one is down. Waiting for just one is fast but can return stale data. Between those extremes lies a tunable choice, and the arithmetic of overlapping sets gives a precise guarantee: a quorum rule that makes stale reads impossible while still tolerating failures.

howItWorks.title: Replicas, writes and reads
howItWorks.text: Keep each item on N replicas. A write is sent to all of them but considered successful once W replicas acknowledge it. A read asks R replicas and takes the newest version among the answers. N, W and R are settings you choose per system, or even per request.

howItWorks.title: The overlap rule: R + W > N
howItWorks.text: If the number of replicas written plus the number read exceeds N, the set that acknowledged the write and the set that answers the read must share at least one replica. That shared replica has the latest write, so the read sees it. Version numbers or timestamps let the reader pick the newest answer.

howItWorks.title: Common settings
howItWorks.text: With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2 you get overlap and tolerate one failure for both reads and writes. W = N, R = 1 makes reads fast but any down replica blocks writes. W = 1, R = N makes writes fast but reads fragile. W = 1 and R = 1 is fastest but only eventually consistent.

howItWorks.title: Availability is the other side
howItWorks.text: A write can proceed while at least W replicas are up, and a read while at least R are up. So you tolerate N − W failed replicas for writes and N − R for reads. Raising W improves consistency of what is stored but lowers write availability, and so on.

howItWorks.title: Quorums are not the whole story
howItWorks.text: Even with overlap, concurrent writes can conflict, sloppy quorums (using stand-in nodes during failures) weaken the guarantee, and a failed write may leave partial copies behind. Systems add read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy and conflict resolution (last write wins, version vectors) to converge replicas.

pros: Tunable consistency, latency and availability for each workload
No single leader is needed, and slow replicas can be ignored
R + W > N gives a simple, checkable guarantee
cons: Reads and writes cost extra round trips to several replicas
Concurrent writes still need conflict resolution
Stale reads are still possible with sloppy quorums or R + W ≤ N
Does not give the ordering guarantees of consensus
whenToUse: Leaderless or multi-leader stores such as Dynamo-style databases (Cassandra, Riak)
When you want to tune consistency per request
Workloads that must stay available when some replicas fail
whenNotToUse: When you need a single agreed order of operations: use consensus
When writes must never be lost or conflict, and last-write-wins is not acceptable
pitfalls: Assuming R + W > N gives linearizability: it does not on its own
Using clock timestamps for 'newest', which skew can get wrong
Forgetting that a failed write may still have reached some replicas
Placing replicas in one failure domain, so a single outage removes the quorum
